newsitem.title: KENYA: Foreign minister says Kenya normal after clashes.
newsitem.headline: Foreign minister says Kenya normal after clashes.

text.p: Foreign Minister Kalonzo Musyoka on Thursday ruled out constitutional reforms before elections and said Kenya was back to normal after clashes in the capital and other parts of the country.

Musyoka told a news conference in Nairobi that Kenya would hold free and fair elections and President Daniel arap Moi had initiated dialogue with leaders to ensure public protests that led to violence in the country last week were not repeated.
He said violence in the Kenyan capital and other towns last week had led to numerous tourist cancellations and planners of international conferences had been also seeking other venues.
But he said his message was "all is back to normal in Kenya and they should come". He gave no details of the cancellations.
Tourism is Kenya's leading foreign exchange earner. Musyoka is also the organising secretary of Moi's ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) party, which has a majority in parliament.
He reiterated Moi's earlier position that comprehensive constitutional reforms were impossible before presidential and parliamentary elections because there was not enough time.

"There are 42 communities in Kenya. Opening up the question of reforms is like opening up the Pandora's box. Every community will want to be heard. All issues are discussible provided there is time and an enabling environment," he said.

"There will be a meeting of minds. There will be a free and fair election. That means that the environment will be conducive for such elections based on criteria agreed by KANU and opposition parties participating," he added.
But an opposition-backed alliance of parties, human rights groups and other bodies demanding constitutional reforms before a general election announced on Thursday new "mass actions" to test Moi.
The constitutional reforms sought by the opposition would reduce the power of Moi, 73 and Kenya's ruler for 19 years. No date for the presidential and parliamentary polls has been set.
Riot police on July 7 violently broke up rallies in Nairobi and several other cities and towns and at least nine people were killed in the worst political violence in Kenya in seven years.
The violence, which closed down Nairobi, was followed by days of student unrest in the city, prompting the closure of two universities followed by the Kenya Polytechnic on Monday.

Moi said on Wednesday he had decided opposition parties would be granted licences for rallies under all but exceptional circumstances while parliament processes a bill to supersede the Public Order Act, which the opposition wants scrapped.

Musyoka said Moi had set the tone by allowing opposition and KANU rallies while Kenyans awaited a repeal of the Public Order Act. But he said such meetings were subject to the protection of rights of others.
He said other steps demanded by the opposition such as free access to state radio and television would be discussed between KANU and the opposition after parliament was dissolved before elections.

He said Moi's separate meetings this week with the Roman Catholic Church head in Kenya, 17 other religious leaders and parliamentary opposition leader Michael Kijana Wamalwa were a signal that the president believed dialogue would prevail.
Senior KANU officials said the ruling party would issue a statement on the demand for constitutional reforms on Thursday.

Musyoka defended force used by police to disperse demonstrators on July 7 as justified. "No one can convince me that police acted out of their mandate," he said. Police beat protesters and fired rubber bullets and tear gas in clashes.
